items.title: Google and Alphabet CEO Sundar Pichai announces leadership changes at Google DeepMind, appointing Demis Hassabis as Chair and Chief Scientist of Alphabet and Koray Kavukcuoglu as SVP of Google DeepMind [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: The next chapter of our AI momentum
items.summary:
Google and Alphabet CEO Sundar Pichai announced organizational changes at Google DeepMind to accelerate AI development and focus on advancing artificial general intelligence (AGI). Demis Hassabis will transition to Chair of Google DeepMind and Chief Scientist of Alphabet, dedicating his efforts to shaping the future of AGI, while Koray Kavukcuoglu will become Senior Vice President of Google DeepMind, overseeing Gemini model development and frontier AI research.

The changes come amid strong momentum for DeepMind's AI models, including high demand for Gemini and Cyber models and significant user engagement with the Gemini app. Additionally, Jeff Dean and Sanjay Ghemawat are launching an independent public benefit corporation to advance machine learning, science, and engineering, with continued collaboration from Google as a founding investor and cloud partner.

items.title: Cloudflare open-sources Cloudflare OS, a customizable platform with agent workspaces and security framework for organizational workflows [ * ] [ ⬢ ]
items.originalTitle: Cloudflare OS: an open platform for agents, apps, and work
items.summary:
Cloudflare has open-sourced a new version of Cloudflare OS, a platform designed to provide every employee with an AI-powered agent workspace tailored to their organization's context, terminology, and systems. The platform enables users to create documents, automate tasks, and build apps that leverage company-specific knowledge and tools, aiming to improve collaboration and efficiency across all functions.

The updated Cloudflare OS addresses challenges from its initial internal deployment, including security and data access controls for shared workspaces. It features an isolated runtime for agents to run code, a governance framework for safe internal data access, and a platform for customizable apps. Organizations can deploy and adapt Cloudflare OS to fit their unique workflows and systems, enabling AI agents to assist with research, task automation, and workflow management within a secure environment.

items.title: Meta releases Muse Code beta powered by Muse Spark 1.2, a coding agent designed for complex software engineering tasks with improved code generation and debugging [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Muse Code and Muse Spark 1.2
items.summary:
Meta has launched Muse Code beta, a terminal-based coding agent powered by its new Muse Spark 1.2 model, aimed at handling complex software engineering tasks across large codebases. Muse Code features persistent asynchronous background agents to improve efficiency and a runtime design that ensures task continuity after crashes. It includes built-in skills for planning, stress-testing, and goal completion.

Muse Spark 1.2 enhances code generation, debugging, and developer workflows through increased training compute and environment diversity, co-trained with Muse Code for optimal performance. The model supports long-horizon coding tasks and self-improvement via generating and grading challenging coding environments. A case study demonstrated Muse Spark 1.2's ability to iteratively optimize GPU kernels over extended periods, achieving significant performance gains. Muse Spark 1.2 is available in Muse Code and Meta Model API with expanded global access.

items.title: Blog explores why niche hobby programming communities resist large language model usage, valuing mastery and learning process over AI-generated code [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Born Against, or why hobby programming communities are against LLM usage
items.summary:
A blog post examines the growing hostility toward large language models (LLMs) in niche hobby programming communities such as OSDev, LangDev, and chess engine developers. These communities prioritize the deep learning process and mastery of difficult domains, viewing LLM-generated code as undermining the craft and effort involved.

The author notes that respect in these groups is earned through years of engagement, sharing knowledge, and understanding why code works rather than just producing working code. While LLMs can serve as tools for experts to amplify their work, using them as surrogates for learning is seen as missing the point and is often met with gatekeeping and skepticism within these communities.

items.title: Neon and Castform demonstrate a 4B open-source model matching GPT-5.6 Sol's retrieval accuracy at 100x lower cost using RL post-training and advanced search infrastructure [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Beating GPT-5.6 Sol on retrieval with 100x cheaper open models
items.summary:
Neon and Castform have developed a 4-billion-parameter open-source model that achieves retrieval accuracy comparable to GPT-5.6 Sol while costing 100 times less per request. This is accomplished through reinforcement learning post-training combined with Neon's Lakebase Postgres search extensions, enabling efficient multi-hop agentic retrieval workflows.

The approach leverages existing enterprise data such as internal documentation and operational databases, converting them into training tasks without extensive manual labeling. Castform manages the reinforcement learning loop to optimize the model's ability to search and retrieve relevant information, addressing common challenges in fine-tuning and infrastructure requirements.

This development suggests that smaller open-source models, when properly post-trained and integrated with advanced search tools, can rival larger closed models in specific tasks like retrieval, potentially reducing costs and latency for enterprise AI applications.

items.title: Prime Agent launches as an open-source self-improving coding agent using Recursive Language Model and Continual Harness abstractions [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Prime Agent: A self-improving RLM agent
items.summary:
Prime Agent is a new open-source coding assistant designed around Recursive Language Model (RLM) and Continual Harness abstractions to enable self-improvement and long-horizon reasoning. It treats context as a variable and allows sub-agent delegation as function calls, enabling persistent access to history and tools within a REPL environment. The Continual Harness abstraction lets the agent modify its own prompts, skills, memory, and sub-agents dynamically, supporting orchestration across sessions and sub-agents.

The system runs a background daemon managing live agent sessions with recoverable worker processes and provides a text-user interface for interaction. Sessions are stored as append-only JSONL files supporting branching and cloning. Prime Agent aims to serve as a general coding assistant, a runtime for autonomous evaluation, and a collaborator for research, compatible with modern open and closed frontier models.

items.title: Researchers find sycophantic AI models affirm user actions 50% more than humans and reduce users' prosocial intentions while increasing dependence [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Sycophantic AI Decreases Prosocial Intentions and Promotes Dependence (2025)
items.summary:
A study analyzing 11 state-of-the-art AI models found that these models excessively agree with users, affirming their actions significantly more than humans do, even when users mention manipulation or deception. Experiments involving over 1,600 participants showed that interacting with sycophantic AI decreased users' willingness to resolve interpersonal conflicts and increased their conviction of being right, despite users rating the AI responses as higher quality and expressing greater trust and willingness to reuse the AI.

The findings suggest that sycophantic AI encourages dependence by validating users uncritically, which may erode judgment and reduce prosocial behavior. This dynamic creates incentives for both users to rely more on such AI and for developers to train models that favor sycophancy, highlighting the need to address these risks explicitly in AI development and deployment.

items.title: Researchers develop adversarially robust neurosymbolic fusion method for pre-trained transformer-based perception models using vector-space geometry without domain knowledge [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Adversarially Robust Abductive Fusion of Pre-trained Transformer-based Perception Models
items.summary: Researchers have introduced a new method to enhance the robustness of pre-trained transformer-based perception models against distributional shifts in novel environments. Their approach replaces traditional majority voting with a metacognitive layer that learns error-detection rules from vector-space geometry derived from each model's training embeddings, avoiding reliance on hand-crafted domain knowledge. This neurosymbolic method frames the fusion of multiple imperfect vision transformer detectors as a consistency-based abduction problem solved via integer programming and heuristics. Evaluated on an aerial imagery benchmark with 15 weather-shifted test sets and six detectors, the method matches majority voting performance on clean data and significantly outperforms it under coordinated label-flipping attacks, maintaining higher F1 scores at high flip rates.

items.originalTitle: The RAIL Principles for Neurosymbolic AI: Reasoning, Assurances, Interfacing and Learning
items.summary:
A recent paper presents the RAIL principles as a unified framework for neurosymbolic AI, which integrates machine learning with symbolic reasoning to enhance AI performance in high-stakes and low-data environments. The authors argue that many existing AI systems, including those not traditionally classified as neurosymbolic, can be understood through this lens, offering a new perspective on AI design.

The framework covers applications such as physics-aware machine learning, neuro-guided search like DeepMind's Alpha-* series, causal learning, and tool-augmented large language models. By applying the RAIL principles, engineers can make more informed decisions about designing and deploying trustworthy AI technologies across various domains.

items.title: Researchers develop NeuMoSync, a neuromodulatory neural network architecture enhancing plasticity and adaptability in continual learning across multiple benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: NeuMoSync: End-to-End Neuromodulatory Control for Plasticity and Adaptability in Continual Learning
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced NeuMoSync, a neural network architecture inspired by the brain's neuromodulatory systems, designed to improve continual learning by dynamically regulating neuron activation and synaptic plasticity. NeuMoSync incorporates neuron-specific modulation and a higher-level module that adapts based on current inputs and the network's state, aiming to address plasticity loss and poor knowledge transfer in sequential task learning.

The architecture was evaluated on diverse continual learning benchmarks, including memorization, concept drift, class-incremental, and domain-incremental tasks, where it demonstrated improved adaptability and plasticity compared to existing methods. Ablation studies confirmed the importance of its components, and analysis revealed interpretable coordination patterns in the modulatory signals. The implementation code is publicly available on GitHub.

items.title: Researchers find that self-distillation with privileged information biases teachers and fails to improve model reasoning across complex tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Privileged, but Biased: How PI-Conditioned Teachers Break Self-Distillation
items.summary:
Researchers examined self-distillation (SD) methods where a teacher model, conditioned on privileged information like reference solutions, supervises a student model that lacks this information. While SD showed gains in simple tasks, the study found it does not improve performance on more difficult tasks such as question answering, mathematics, coding, and multi-turn tool use, with validation accuracy often degrading despite decreasing per-token loss.

The failure is attributed to bias introduced by privileged information, which causes the teacher's targets to favor specific solution trajectories rather than general correctness. This bias leads the student model to focus on low-information tokens and penalize necessary reasoning hesitation, resulting in a less decisive model that does not improve reasoning ability. The findings suggest that as a standalone objective without reward signals, self-distillation optimizes a training signal disconnected from actual task success.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.04794v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Self-distillation (SD) has emerged as a compute-efficient alternative to reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards: a self-teacher, conditioned on privileged information (PI) about the answer such as a reference solution, supplies dense per-token supervision to a student that never sees it. Reported gains, however, come almost exclusively from narrow, low-difficulty settings, leaving open a basic question: as a lone objective, with no reward term, does SD teach anything? We reproduce SDPO's reported gains in its easy setting, then apply the identical setup to difficult tasks and find that it does not. Across question answering, mathematics, coding, and multi-turn agentic tool use, across reasoning modes, model sizes, and forms of PI, and under both the SDPO and OPSD recipes, the per-token loss falls steadily while validation accuracy does not improve and typically degrades. We explain this failure through a single causal chain from the loss to the model it produces. The chain begins with PI bias: having seen one particular reference solution, the teacher's per-token target is pulled toward that trajectory rather than toward correctness in general, an effect we quantify with a PI Bias Score. Trained to match this target everywhere, the student's objective becomes nearly blind to whether a rollout is correct, and the loss it assigns falls mostly on low-information tokens like stopwords, punctuation, uncertainty markers, rather than those that determine the answer; within correct rollouts the exploratory tokens incur the highest divergence, so it penalizes the hesitation that reasoning requires. The result is a flatter, less decisive student that is no better at reasoning: as a lone objective, SD optimizes a signal decoupled from task success.

items.title: Researchers introduce WorldCycle, a self-verifiable reinforcement learning framework using reversible action cycles to improve long-horizon video world models and reduce state returning drift by up to 44% [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: WorldCycle: Self-Verifiable Reinforcement Learning for Long-Horizon Video World Models
items.summary: Researchers present WorldCycle, a reinforcement learning framework designed to enhance interactive video world models for long-horizon planning by addressing compounding errors through self-verification using reversible action cycles. This approach constructs closed action cycles from ordinary sequences and optimizes spatial closure and temporal consistency rewards to enforce accurate state transitions without relying on ground-truth future states. The team also released CycleBench, a benchmark for evaluating state-returning ability under complex action structures, demonstrating that WorldCycle improves composite-action accuracy nearly fourfold compared to base models. This work provides a foundation for more physically grounded and reliable world models in video-based reinforcement learning.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.04964v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Interactive video world models are essential for long-horizon planning and exploration, yet they suffer from compounding errors. Post-training methods such as reinforcement learning (RL) can improve these models, but they hit a verification bottleneck: for arbitrary action sequences, no ground-truth future state exists to measure long-term drift. Our key insight is that reversible action cycles make this verification possible: a sequence composed with its inverse must analytically return to the initial state, yielding annotation-free supervision on long-horizon correctness. Building on this, we introduce WorldCycle, a self-verifiable RL framework that constructs closed action cycles and their repeated executions from ordinary action sequences, and optimizes two complementary rewards: a spatial closure reward enforcing symmetry between mirrored forward and reverse segments, and a temporal consistency reward aligning states across repeated cycle executions. These rewards force the model to learn actions as consistent state operators rather than memorized temporal patterns, and extend naturally to out-of-distribution composite action cycles that the base model handles poorly. We further release CycleBench, a diagnostic benchmark for state-returning ability under complex action structures. WorldCycle reduces state returning drift by up to 44% and lifts composite-action accuracy nearly 4x over the base model, providing a vital foundation for physically grounded world models.

items.title: Researchers report 41-day live challenge results for EU-AI Act compliant short-term load forecasting pipeline on German transmission-grid load [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Short-term load forecasting under EU-AI Act Requirements in Safety-Critical Environments: Results from a 41-day live challenge on the aggregated German transmission-grid load
items.summary:
A 41-day live challenge evaluated a short-term load forecasting (STLF) pipeline designed to meet EU-AI Act requirements for safety-critical environments, focusing on the aggregated German transmission-grid load. The pipeline, based on the open-source Python library spotforecast2-safe, predicts 24 hourly load values using ENTSO-E data and incorporates anomaly detection, gap-aware data preparation, calendar and weather covariates, recursive multi-step forecasting, and hyperparameter tuning. It outperformed the official ENTSO-E day-ahead forecast baseline during the challenge.

The study highlights that STLF is not only an accuracy challenge but also a software engineering and compliance issue due to legal requirements for determinism, reproducibility, and auditability in critical infrastructure. Transparent, low-cost, and auditable local models demonstrated competitive performance compared to large, energy-intensive pre-trained foundation models. The challenge infrastructure, submission history, and final leaderboard are publicly available for further analysis.

items.title: Researchers introduce OctoLong pipeline to enhance long-context language model training with cross-repository code contexts, improving code understanding and long-range retrieval [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: OctoLong: Mid-Training On Cross-Repository Code Contexts Enhances Long-Context Modeling
items.summary:
Researchers have developed OctoLong, a context engineering pipeline that uses an AST parser, language server backend, and package manager to recursively retrieve code references, creating dependency-rich code contexts millions of tokens long. They trained OctoLong-Instruct, a suite of long-context open language models ranging from 600 million to 14 billion parameters, using a 50 billion token mixture including 6.2 billion tokens from OctoLong code contexts, followed by instruction tuning.

Experimental evaluations against 18 state-of-the-art open-weight long-context language models show that replacing 12% of traditional context-extension corpora with OctoLong data significantly improves long-range retrieval, long-term state tracking, repository-level code understanding, and downstream agentic tasks, while also enhancing API usage in short-context coding scenarios.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.05141v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Context lengths of language models (LMs) have dramatically increased, driven by the demands for in-context learning, self-improvement, and long-horizon agentic workflows. Existing long-context corpora, however, are dominated by books, academic articles, and code repositories, which are finite resources and often scarce in long-distance dependencies. In this work, we introduce OctoLong, a context engineering pipeline that instruments an AST parser, a language server backend, and a package manager to facilitate the recursive retrieval of code references, enabling the curation of dependency-rich code contexts of millions of tokens in length. We then train OctoLong-Instruct, a suite of capable long-context open LMs, derived from base models ranging in size from 600M to 14B parameters, via context-extension mid-training on a ~50B-token mixture containing ~6.2B tokens of OctoLong code contexts, followed by ~10B tokens of instruction tuning. Our training ablations and experimental evaluations against 18 state-of-the-art open-weight long-context LMs show that supplanting just 12% of traditional context-extension corpora with OctoLong data yields substantial gains in long-range retrieval, long-term state tracking, repository-level code understanding, and downstream agentic tasks, while also enhancing API usage in short-context coding scenarios.

items.title: C2MOE proposes a consistency and complementarity-guided mixture of experts framework for incomplete multimodal emotion recognition, improving robustness and imputation accuracy [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: C$^2$MOE: Consistency and Complementarity-guided Mixture of Experts for Incomplete Multimodal Emotion Learning
items.summary:
Researchers introduce C2MOE, a novel framework addressing missing modalities in multimodal emotion recognition by factorizing knowledge into consistency and complementarity components using interaction-aware experts. The approach combines representation learning and missing modality imputation through a dual-branch prediction mechanism that aligns imputed features with joint distributions and exploits modality-unique cues.

C2MOE employs a learnable reweighting module to dynamically fuse expert outputs, enhancing robustness and adaptability. Experiments on multiple benchmarks demonstrate that C2MOE outperforms state-of-the-art methods across various missing-modality scenarios, validating its effectiveness and generalization capabilities.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.04013v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent advances in Multimodal Emotion Recognition in Conversations (MERC) highlight its reliance on complete multimodal inputs. However, real-world data often suffer from missing modalities due to transmission errors or user behavior, severely degrading model performance. Existing methods enhance robustness via cross-modal consistency learning but largely ignore modality complementarity, leading to biased reconstructions. To address this limitation, we propose C$2$MOE, a novel Consistency and Complementarity-guided Mixture of Experts framework for incomplete multimodal emotion learning. Our approach unifies representation learning and missing modality imputation within a principled information-theoretic framework. Specifically, multimodal knowledge is factorized into consistency and complementarity components via interaction-aware experts. Consistency is captured by maximizing cross-modal predictability, while complementarity is preserved by maximizing conditional entropy between modalities. Building upon this decomposition, C$2$MOE introduces a dual-branch prediction mechanism for robust imputation under missing modalities. The consistency branch aligns imputed features with the joint distribution by minimizing uncertainty, and the complementarity branch exploits modality-unique cues via entropy maximization. Finally, C$2$MOE employs a learnable reweighting module that dynamically assigns importance scores to each expert's output, yielding a robust and adaptive fusion for imputation. Extensive experiments on multiple MERC benchmarks demonstrate that C$2$MOE consistently surpasses state-of-the-art methods across various missing-modality settings, validating its robustness and generalization.

items.title: Researchers develop Hamming-Lipschitz stability theory for subdominant ultrametrics, showing sparse edits affect ultrametric entries only via minimum spanning tree paths [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: On Hamming-Lipschitz Type Stability of the Subdominant (Minmax) Ultrametric: Theory and Simple Proofs
items.summary:
The subdominant (minmax) ultrametric, used as a tree-structured summary of dissimilarity matrices and induced by single-linkage clustering, has classical stability bounds that poorly handle sparse perturbations. Researchers developed an \(\ell_0\)-type stability theory demonstrating that changes in pairwise ultrametric values occur only if their tree path crosses an edited edge or a newly exposed cut from an off-tree edge, leading to precise bounds on the number of affected ultrametric entries.

The analysis includes sharpness results proving that the dependence on tree geometry is unavoidable, with explicit examples where a single edited distance can change a quadratic number of ultrametric entries. A conditional near-additivity principle for multiple edits is also established. Experiments on deep-embedding graphs indicate that these structural scores can diagnose vulnerabilities in hierarchical representations.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.04014v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The subdominant (minmax) ultrametric is a canonical tree-structured summary of a dissimilarity matrix, arising equivalently as the ultrametric induced by single-linkage clustering. While its classical stability theory is usually formulated in $\ell_\infty$ or Gromov--Hausdorff terms, such bounds are poorly suited to sparse perturbations that alter only a few pairwise distances. We develop an $\ell_0$-type stability theory for this operator. Our analysis shows that sparse edits propagate only through the minimum spanning tree (MST): a pairwise ultrametric value can change only if its tree path crosses an edited edge or a cut newly exposed by an edited off-tree edge. This yields a sharp per-edit exposed-cut score and a tree-only global envelope, leading to Hamming--Lipschitz bounds on the number of ultrametric entries that can change. We also prove sharpness results showing that this dependence on tree geometry is unavoidable: under strict cut separation the tree-edge bound is attained exactly, and for off-tree edits there are explicit families in which one edited distance changes $\Theta(n^2)$ ultrametric entries. In addition, we prove a conditional near-additivity principle for multiple edits under certified large per-edit changed regions and negligible aggregate overlap. Experiments on deep-embedding graphs show that the resulting structural scores provide useful vulnerability diagnostics for hierarchical representations.

items.title: Researchers develop AI-driven multimodal framework to uncover latent pathways linking socioeconomic disadvantage, psychosocial factors, and cardiometabolic multimorbidity using All of Us data [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: AI-driven Multimodal Representation Learning for Latent Mediation Structure Discovery of Socioeconomic Disadvantage, Psychosocial Factors, and Cardiometabolic Multimorbidity: Insights from the All of Us Research Program
items.summary:
Researchers created an AI-based multimodal mediation framework integrating socioeconomic, psychosocial, clinical, laboratory, behavioral, and genomic data from 20,804 participants in the All of Us Research Program to study links between social disadvantage and multimorbidity. They used variational autoencoders to derive latent representations of each data domain and performed mediation analyses to identify indirect associations among socioeconomic disadvantage, psychosocial vulnerability, and cardiometabolic multimorbidity.

The strongest indirect association involved a latent socioeconomic disadvantage dimension, a psychosocial vulnerability dimension characterized by poorer mental health and social well-being, and a cardiometabolic multimorbidity dimension associated with conditions like hypertension, diabetes, and heart disease. Bootstrap analyses confirmed the stability of this pathway. The study demonstrates how AI representation learning can elucidate complex relationships across high-dimensional multimodal health data.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.04016v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Social disadvantage is associated with multimorbidity, but the pathways linking social conditions to disease burden remain poorly understood. We developed an AI-driven multimodal mediation framework that integrates socioeconomic, psychosocial, clinical, laboratory, behavioral, and genomic data from the All of Us Research Program. Modality-specific variational autoencoders were used to derive latent representations of each data domain, and mediation analyses were subsequently performed in latent space to evaluate indirect associations between socioeconomic disadvantage, psychosocial factors, and multimorbidity. The final analytic cohort included 20,804 participants with complete multimodal data. Across 800 exposure--mediator--outcome combinations, mediation signals were concentrated within a small number of latent dimensions. The strongest indirect association linked a socioeconomic disadvantage dimension, a psychosocial vulnerability dimension, and a cardiometabolic multimorbidity dimension (NIE = 0.002517). The psychosocial dimension was characterized by poorer mental health, greater loneliness, lower social well-being, and lower health literacy, whereas the outcome dimension was associated with hypertension, diabetes, hyperlipidemia, obesity, chronic kidney disease, and heart disease. Bootstrap analyses supported the stability of the leading pathway. These findings suggest that psychosocial vulnerability was strongly represented in the dominant latent pathway linking socioeconomic disadvantage and cardiometabolic multimorbidity. More broadly, the proposed framework illustrates how AI-based representation learning can be used to investigate complex relationships across high-dimensional multimodal health data.

items.title: Researchers develop a trust-region framework for adaptive moment estimation in stochastic gradient optimization, introducing Gmake with moment constraints from order 2 to 4 [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: A Trust-region Framework for Moment Estimation
items.summary:
Researchers propose a trust-region framework to analyze adaptive moment estimation methods like Adam in stochastic gradient optimization, constraining update steps by moment constraints of order p between 2 and 4. This framework leads to a family of learning-rate mechanisms based on second-moment and normalized p-th moment estimations, with p=4 involving kurtosis-like estimation, unified under the mechanism called Gmake.

items.title: Researchers introduce a Lindblad-inspired multi-timescale reservoir computing model with separable rotation and dissipation for improved temporal learning and stability [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Lindblad-Inspired Multi-Timescale Reservoir Computing with Separable Rotation and Dissipation
items.summary: Researchers propose a new reservoir computing architecture inspired by Lindblad dynamics that separates reversible mixing and irreversible forgetting through independently tunable rotation and dissipation parameters. This design preserves stability without spectral-radius rescaling and allows explicit control over memory and mixing in echo-state networks. The model was evaluated against various reservoir types and a gated recurrent unit across multiple benchmarks, achieving top performance on tasks like bounded NARMA-20 and Lorenz-63 forecasting. Ablation studies highlight that rotation enhances state diversity while dissipation enables controlled forgetting and better predictive conditioning, offering an interpretable and stable recurrent framework.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.04028v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Echo-state networks enable efficient temporal learning by fixing the recurrent dynamics and training only a linear readout. However, conventional reservoirs typically accommodate signal mixing, memory retention, and stability within a single random recurrent matrix. Existing structured designs improve topology, norm preservation, leakage, or depth, but generally do not provide separate modal control of reversible mixing and irreversible forgetting together with a direct global stability guarantee. We introduce a classical Lindblad-inspired multi-timescale reservoir that bridges open-system dynamical principles with structured state-space modeling. The recurrent operator is assembled from exactly discretized damped rotational modes, so rotation and decay become independent design variables governing phase mixing and memory loss. Orthogonal mode mixing preserves normality, while the decay spectrum directly determines the echo-state stability margin without post-hoc spectral-radius rescaling. We evaluate the method over ten aligned seeds against standard, leaky, deep, orthogonal, cycle, and next-generation reservoirs, together with a compact trained gated recurrent unit, across linear memory, nonlinear recurrence, chaotic forecasting, delayed logic, and real sensor calibration. Across the benchmark suite, the proposed reservoir achieves the best fixed-reservoir performance on bounded NARMA-20 and the lowest mean error on Lorenz-63, matches the strongest linear-memory result, and remains broadly competitive across broad range of benchmarks. Ablation studies show that rotation increases state diversity, whereas dissipation provides controlled forgetting and improves predictive conditioning. The resulting framework offers an interpretable recurrent architecture in which mixing, memory, and stability are explicit and independently tunable design variables.

items.title: Researchers fine-tune open-source diffusion models for nuclear energy text-to-image generation, improving accuracy over general-purpose and commercial AI systems [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: NuclearDiffusion: Text-to-Image Foundation Models for Learning Nuclear Energy Concepts
items.summary:
Researchers conducted a systematic study on adapting text-to-image AI models for nuclear engineering by fine-tuning three open-source diffusion models using a curated dataset of 1,000 captioned nuclear energy images. The fine-tuned models were evaluated quantitatively and qualitatively, showing substantial fidelity improvements for Stable Diffusion XL, limited gains for SD-v3.5-Medium, and no improvement for Flux.1, highlighting the importance of model architecture in adaptation effectiveness.

The study also compared these fine-tuned models against leading commercial systems like GPT-Image-2, Gemini-3.1-Flash-Image, and Midjourney, finding that while commercial models generate convincing images for broad nuclear concepts, they often fail on specialized engineering prompts. The fine-tuned open-source models produced more accurate and technically consistent outputs, suggesting domain-specific fine-tuning as a viable approach for developing reliable generative AI tools in specialized fields.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.04030v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) has transformed text-to-image synthesis, yet its ability to represent specialized engineering domains remains largely unexplored. As an exmaple in nuclear engineering, general-purpose foundation models frequently generate physically incorrect or conceptually inconsistent images because they lack domain-specific knowledge. This work presents one of the first systematic studies of domain adaptation for nuclear text-to-image generation through fine-tuning of open-source diffusion models. We curate a dataset of 1,000 captioned nuclear energy images spanning reactors, fuel cycles, radiation, and related concepts, and use it to fine-tune three state-of-the-art open-source models: Stable Diffusion XL (SDXL), SD-v3.5-Medium, and the flow-matching Flux.1 model. Their performance is evaluated using both quantitative image-similarity metrics and qualitative expert assessment against the corresponding zero-shot models. Fine-tuning substantially improves the fidelity of SDXL, provides only limited gains for SD-v3.5-Medium, and yields no measurable improvement for Flux.1, demonstrating that adaptation effectiveness depends strongly on the underlying generative architecture rather than model scale alone. We further compare the fine-tuned models against three leading commercial systems--GPT-Image-2, Gemini-3.1-Flash-Image, and Midjourney. Although GPT-Image-2 and Gemini generate convincing images for broad nuclear concepts, they frequently fail on specialized engineering prompts, where the fine-tuned open-source models produce more accurate and technically consistent outputs. These results establish domain-specific fine-tuning as a practical pathway for developing trustworthy generative AI tools for domain-specific applications.

items.originalTitle: Robust and Personalized Federated Learning for Aircraft-Engine Prognostics under Benign and Adversarial Client Heterogeneity
items.summary: This study investigates federated learning approaches that allow aircraft fleet operators to collaboratively train models predicting engine remaining useful life without sharing raw data. It addresses challenges from benign heterogeneity, where operators experience different conditions, and adversarial heterogeneity, where some submit poisoned updates. Using a multi-task convolutional neural network on a non-IID partition of the C-MAPSS benchmark, the researchers compare remedies for benign heterogeneity and test attacks against aggregation methods, including a sensor-value backdoor designed to mask engine degradation.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.04045v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Federated learning (FL) enables aircraft fleet operators to jointly train remaining-useful-life (RUL) models from engine sensor telemetry without sharing raw data. This study examines two complementary challenges: benign heterogeneity, where honest operators observe different operating conditions and fault modes, and adversarial heterogeneity, where compromised operators submit poisoned updates. We conduct a controlled, safety-oriented evaluation using a multi-task one-dimensional convolutional neural network and a structurally non-IID partition of the Commercial Modular Aero-Propulsion System Simulation (C-MAPSS) benchmark. We compare four remedies for benign heterogeneity and evaluate five attacks against four aggregation methods, including a physically motivated sensor-value backdoor designed to mask engine degradation. Shared-representation personalization closes approximately 70% of the local-to-centralized root-mean-square-error gap, compared with 21% for proximal regularization and 10% for server-side reweighting. The backdoor achieves a 94.9% attack success rate against standard averaging while leaving clean accuracy statistically unchanged, demonstrating that accuracy alone cannot certify model safety and that attack success must be evaluated explicitly. Krum reduces attack success by an order of magnitude and is the only evaluated aggregator that withstands coordinated attackers, whereas personalization alone provides no protection. Combining personalization with robust aggregation restores robustness (2.8% attack success) with only a small accuracy cost, revealing a trade-off between robust update selection and collaborative representation learning. Results remain consistent across client counts and on a harder six-condition dataset. Code and data partitions are released for reproducibility.

items.title: Researchers propose temporal QBER based machine learning framework to detect and classify stealthy eavesdropping attacks in BB84 quantum key distribution systems [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Beyond the QBER Threshold: A Temporal QBER Based Machine Learning Framework for Multi Attack Detection in BB84 QKD
items.summary: Conventional BB84 Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) systems use a fixed 11% Quantum Bit Error Rate (QBER) threshold to detect eavesdropping, but stealthy attacks can evade this detection. This study introduces a machine learning framework that analyzes 63 physics-informed temporal features of QBER to improve detection accuracy and classify multiple attack types under noisy and lossy conditions. The framework, tested with Random Forest, XGBoost, and SVM classifiers, significantly outperforms the traditional threshold method, reducing false negatives from 84.77% to 1.98% and achieving up to 88% accuracy with explainable feature importance.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.04047v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Conventional BB84 Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) systems rely on a fixed 11% Quantum Bit Error Rate (QBER) threshold to detect eavesdropping. However, stealthy attacks can remain below this threshold while still compromising channel security. This paper proposes a temporal QBER based machine learning framework for detecting and classifying eavesdropping attacks in BB84 QKD systems. Rather than relying on average session level QBER, the framework extracts 63 physics-informed temporal features capturing burst behavior, temporal instability, basis dependent asymmetry, and QBER loss interactions. Random Forest, XGBoost, and Support Vector Machine with a Radial Basis Function kernel (SVM-RBF) classifiers are evaluated on seven eavesdropping attacks and a normal channel scenario under noisy and lossy conditions. Averaged over ten independent runs, XGBoost achieves the best performance with 88.01% (0.47%) accuracy and a macro F1 score of 0.8803, while SVM-RBF performs comparably, confirming the robustness of the proposed features. Evaluated as a binary attack-versus-normal detector for comparison with conventional monitoring, a fixed 11% QBER threshold achieves only 25.82% accuracy with a False Negative Rate (FNR) of 0.8477, whereas the proposed framework reduces the FNR to 0.0198, substantially improving detection of stealthy attacks that evade threshold-based monitoring. SHapley Additive exPlanations based (SHAP) explainability shows that physics-informed temporal and channel derived features are highly discriminative for identifying eavesdropping strategies. These results demonstrate that temporal QBER driven machine learning provides an accurate, explainable, and practical framework for multi attack security monitoring in BB84 QKD systems.

items.title: Researchers introduce Recurrent Residual Quantization, a post-training method enabling multi-precision weight representations for large language models from a single checkpoint [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Recurrent Residual Quantization: A Progressive Multi-Precision Representation for LLMs
items.summary: Researchers propose Recurrent Residual Quantization (RRQ), a post-training quantization framework that represents large language model weights as a low-bit quantized base plus sequential quantized residuals, allowing multiple effective precisions from one checkpoint. Starting from a 2-bit model, RRQ progressively adds 2-bit residuals to build 4-, 6-, and 8-bit representations without requiring calibration or joint multi-bit optimization. In tests on six recent large language models, RRQ achieved competitive accuracy at 6 and 8 bits, with variable results at 4 bits, and constructed a full 2-/4-/6-/8-bit package 3.3 times faster than a comparable method in a Qwen3-8B setup. The code will be publicly released upon publication.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.04048v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Serving large language models (LLMs) under diverse deployment constraints requires flexible trade-offs between accuracy, memory footprint, and throughput. However, conventional quantization methods typically require a separate checkpoint for each target bit-width. We introduce Recurrent Residual Quantization (RRQ), a post-training quantization (PTQ) framework that represents weights as a low-bit quantized base together with a sequence of quantized residual corrections, enabling multiple effective precisions from a single checkpoint. Starting from a 2-bit model obtained via post-training quantization (PTQ) or round-to-nearest (RTN), RRQ progressively adds lightweight 2-bit residuals generated via RTN to construct 4-, 6-, and 8-bit representations. The method is calibration-free and avoids joint multi-bit optimization. In our Qwen3-8B setup, the full all-RTN 2-/4-/6-/8-bit package is constructed in 1,293 seconds, 3.3 times faster than the measured MatGPTQ construction. Experiments on six recent LLMs show competitive accuracy at 6 and 8 bits, with model-dependent behavior at 4 bits. The code will be made publicly available upon publication.

items.summary:

Unlike traditional methods that suppress modality inconsistencies, MACH represents these disagreements as distinct relational structures through hierarchical prototype hypergraphs, progressively composing unimodal to trimodal abstractions.

MACH employs separate pathways for agreement and conflict, combined via a feature-wise, sample-adaptive arbitration mechanism to preserve informative disagreements while reducing noise. The model is optimized progressively to stabilize its hierarchical structure before joint learning. Experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate MACH's effectiveness, with analyses confirming the importance of its hierarchical composition, semantic refinement, and agreement-conflict arbitration components.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.04054v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Multimodal intent recognition requires understanding not only what textual, acoustic, and visual signals share, but also how they disagree. Such disagreement is frequently class-informative; for example, lexical positivity accompanied by incongruent vocal or facial behavior may indicate sarcasm or taunting, yet most fusion methods either encourage modality alignment or treat inconsistency as uncertainty to be suppressed. We propose MACH (Modality Agreement- and Conflict-aware prototype Hypergraph), a hierarchical prototype-hypergraph framework that represents multimodal agreement and conflict as distinct, recurring relational structures. MACH progressively composes unimodal representations into bimodal and trimodal abstractions. At each applicable level, modality-composition anchors activate sparse agreement prototype hypergraphs that capture reusable consensus patterns, while a separate conflict pathway maps cross-modal discrepancies to dedicated conflict prototype hypergraphs. The two pathways are combined through a feature-wise, sample-adaptive arbitration mechanism, enabling the model to preserve informative disagreement while suppressing incidental modality noise. A progressive optimization strategy stabilizes the interdependent hierarchy before joint agreement-conflict learning. Experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed formulation, while component and robustness analyses validate the distinct roles of hierarchical composition, prototype-mediated semantic refinement, and agreement-conflict arbitration.

items.title: LaPrune introduces a differentiable layer for controllable sparsity with exact budget control and normalized second moment at million-scale models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: LaPrune: Controllable Differentiable Sparsity at Million Scale
items.summary:
LaPrune is a new differentiable layer designed to control sparsity in large-scale models by preserving the selected mass and managing the normalized second moment. It uses a LapSum barrier and a normalized second-moment constraint to transition masks from dense equal-mass allocations toward hard top-k selections, enabling gradient flow where traditional hard selection blocks it.

The method provides a population prediction of the saturated fraction, a near-binary limiting behavior, and a worst-case guarantee on the near-zero fraction. Its normalized hardness parameter remains invariant to score scale, addressing limitations of fixed LapSum temperature approaches.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.04057v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Top-$k$ selection determines which components of a sparse model remain active. Hard selection blocks gradients, while continuous relaxations often couple mask hardness to the selected mass. We introduce LaPrune, a mathematically exact-budget differentiable layer that controls the normalized second moment while preserving the selected mass. A LapSum barrier preserves the selection mass, and a normalized second-moment constraint moves the mask from a dense equal-mass allocation toward hard top-$k$ at each budget. We derive a population prediction of the saturated fraction, a near-binary limiting law, and a tight worst-case guarantee on the near-zero fraction. The normalized hardness parameter is invariant to score scale, while a fixed LapSum temperature is not.

items.title: Researchers introduce SJEPA, a hybrid symbolic-neural framework for learning compact latent dynamics with predictive representations and symbolic descriptions [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: SJEPA: Learning Elegant Latent Dynamics with Hybrid Symbolic-Neural Predictors
items.summary:
Researchers present SJEPA, a reconstruction-free joint-embedding predictive architecture that combines symbolic laws with neural corrections to learn predictive representations whose dynamics admit compact symbolic descriptions. The framework aims to balance predictive fidelity, representation quality, and symbolic parsimony by enforcing constraints that preserve informative predictive coordinates and favor low-complexity symbolic-neural transitions.

In controlled pendulum experiments, SJEPA's joint learning approach discovers simpler symbolic dynamics with lower long-horizon rollout errors compared to post-hoc fitting, while regularization helps maintain symbolic mechanisms under grammar misspecification. The study formalizes induced-dynamics complexity and highlights trade-offs among predictive accuracy, representation collapse, and symbolic-neural allocation in latent dynamics modeling.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.04060v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Joint-embedding predictive architectures learn abstract states by predicting target embeddings from context embeddings, but their transition models are typically opaque neural maps. We introduce SJEPA, a reconstruction-free JEPA framework that learns predictive representations whose induced dynamics admit compact symbolic descriptions. Its hybrid transition combines a symbolic law with a regularised neural correction for dynamics outside the selected grammar. The central principle is to learn the simplest adequate dynamics: representation constraints preserve informative, non-collapsed predictive coordinates, while operator compression favours low-complexity symbolic-neural transitions that remain predictively adequate. We formalise this principle through induced-dynamics complexity, analyse predictive-coordinate non-identifiability, and show that unconstrained operator compression creates a direct shortcut to representation collapse. The framework supports both alternating representation-equation learning and symbolic dynamics fitted to fixed representations. In controlled pendulum experiments, joint learning discovers substantially simpler symbolic dynamics with lower long-horizon rollout error and divergence than post-hoc fitting, while an unconstrained one-step diagnostic realises the predicted collapse shortcut. Under grammar misspecification, correction regularisation preserves the representable symbolic mechanism and directs the neural component towards residual dynamics. The results expose a controllable trade-off among predictive fidelity, representation quality, symbolic parsimony, and symbolic-neural allocation.

items.title: Researchers propose FBID, an adaptive personalized federated learning framework using server-side control to improve out-of-distribution attack detection in heterogeneous IoT networks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: FBID: Adaptive Personalized Federated Learning for Robust Out-of-Distribution Attack Detection in IoT Networks
items.summary:
Researchers introduce Federated Bandit Intrusion Detection (FBID), a personalized federated learning framework designed to enhance intrusion detection in heterogeneous IoT environments by addressing over-personalization issues in out-of-distribution (OOD) attack detection. FBID employs a contextual multi-armed bandit at the server to dynamically adjust each client's local training intensity and uses a trust-based blending mechanism to balance global and local model knowledge.

Extensive experiments on the CICIoT2023 dataset under diverse client distributions and OOD stress-test conditions demonstrate that FBID improves individual client OOD detection rates by up to 7.66% and F1 scores by up to 5.08% relative to the strongest baseline, while also enhancing robustness against previously unseen attack classes.

Extensive experiments on the CICIoT2023 dataset under diverse client distributions and OOD stress-test conditions demonstrate that FBID improves individual client OOD detection rates by up to 7.66% and F1 scores by up to 5.08% relative to the strongest baseline, while also enhancing robustness against previously unseen attack classes.
items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.04073v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Personalized Federated Learning (PFL) has emerged as a promising solution for intrusion detection in heterogeneous IoT environments, as it can improve local adaptation under highly Non-Independent and Identically Distributed (non-IID) data distributions. However, existing PFL methods often rely on client-side self-adjustment, which may lead to over-personalization and substantial degradation in out-of-distribution (OOD) attack detection. In this paper, we propose Federated Bandit Intrusion Detection (FBID), a novel adaptive PFL framework to address this limitation through server-side personalization control. In particular, FBID employs a contextual multi-armed bandit at the server to dynamically regulate each client's local training intensity according to its observed behavior and update quality. Moreover, FBID introduces a trust-based blending mechanism to derive client-specific interpolation coefficients between the global and local models, thereby preserving global attack-detection knowledge while still allowing beneficial local specialization. Through extensive experiments on the CICIoT2023 dataset under heterogeneous client distributions and OOD stress-test settings, we show that FBID improves individual client OOD Detection Rate (DR) by up to 7.66% and F1-Score (F1) by up to 5.08% (relative) over the strongest stable baseline, while also improving robustness to previously unseen attack classes.

items.title: Researchers propose NOVA-KV, a vector quantization method for KV cache in long-context LLM decoding that preserves attention accuracy at two bits per element [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Spend Bits Where Queries Look: KV Cache Vector Quantization with Attention-Preserving Transforms
items.summary:
Researchers introduce NOVA-KV, a method that reduces key-value (KV) cache size in long-context large language model (LLM) decoding to improve throughput by preserving attention products with efficient vector quantization. The approach formulates KV cache quantization as a transform coding problem, deriving optimal non-orthogonal transforms from calibration statistics to minimize attention distortion while meeting fixed per-token bit constraints.

NOVA-KV applies mean-squared error-optimal vector quantizers to transformed key coefficients and groups coefficients into equal-volume partitions to achieve variable-rate optimum with equal-size codebooks. At two bits per element, this method recovers most of the long-context retrieval accuracy lost by previous scalar quantization techniques without sacrificing throughput.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.04074v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Long-context LLM decoding reads the key-value (KV) cache at every step. Loading it takes longer than computing attention over it, so throughput is bandwidth-bound. Hence, reducing the cache size can raise both decoding speed and serving capacity. The challenge is to reduce cache size while preserving the attention products, keeping reconstruction cheap, and using a fixed per-token bit count. At two bits per element, the most competitive methods rely on orthogonal transforms. However, existing techniques are either data-oblivious or use the query statistics without deriving the transform from a distortion criterion. Moreover, they rely on transforms built on top of random or Hadamard rotations, which equalize variances across entries rather than compacting energy, and fixed-width scalar quantizers, which are suboptimal at low rates. In this paper, we formulate KV cache quantization as a transform coding problem in which distortion is the error in the attention products. We derive closed-form optimal transforms for keys and values from calibration statistics, under a high-resolution model. We show that the optimal key transform is not orthogonal and satisfies a generalized Parseval relation: the attention-aware distortion becomes mean-squared error (MSE) in the transform domain. Thus, we can use MSE-optimal vector quantizers applied directly to the transformed key coefficients. To meet the fixed-width layout requirement, we show that grouping coefficients into equal-volume partitions makes equal-size codebooks attain the variable-rate optimum under the same high-resolution model. At two bits per element, our method, termed NOVA-KV, recovers most of the long-context retrieval accuracy lost by scalar quantization methods at comparable throughput.

items.title: Researchers propose spatiotemporal graph Transformer for traffic forecasting in edge computing, outperforming recurrent graph models on real-world cellular data [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Spatiotemporal Graph Transformer for Traffic Intelligence in Edge Computing
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a spatiotemporal graph Transformer framework to improve traffic forecasting in edge computing environments, where service demand changes dynamically across space and time. The model combines graph neural networks to capture spatial correlations among service regions with Transformer-based self-attention to learn long-range temporal dependencies, addressing limitations of existing recurrent forecasting methods in modeling long-term traffic evolution.

Extensive experiments on a real-world cellular network dataset show that the proposed graph Transformer consistently outperforms recurrent graph-based baselines such as GCN-RNN, GCN-LSTM, and GCN-GRU across multiple forecasting horizons. The improved forecasts enable more effective proactive resource provisioning and reduce overload risks compared to reactive management strategies, highlighting the potential of graph-enhanced attention mechanisms for intelligent and adaptive edge computing systems.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.04075v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Accurate traffic forecasting is essential for proactive resource management in edge computing, where service demand evolves dynamically across both space and time. In practical cellular edge systems, traffic exhibits strong spatial correlations among neighboring service regions and long-range temporal dependencies driven by user mobility and application behavior. Existing recurrent forecasting approaches can capture short-term dynamics but often struggle to model long-horizon traffic evolution under non-stationary conditions. To address this challenge, we propose a spatiotemporal graph Transformer framework that jointly models spatial interactions and temporal dependencies for traffic forecasting in edge computing. The framework employs graph neural networks to capture spatial correlations among service regions and leverages Transformer-based self-attention to learn long-range temporal patterns from historical traffic observations. By decoupling spatial representation learning from temporal reasoning, the proposed approach provides an effective mechanism for large-scale spatiotemporal traffic modeling. Extensive experiments on a real-world cellular network dataset demonstrate that the proposed graph Transformer consistently outperforms recurrent graph-based baselines, including GCN-RNN, GCN-LSTM, and GCN-GRU models, across multiple forecasting horizons. The resulting forecasts enable more effective proactive resource provisioning and reduce overload risk compared with reactive management strategies. These results highlight the potential of graph-enhanced attention mechanisms for building intelligent and adaptive edge computing systems.

items.title: Researchers propose Out-Of-The-Loop Multi-Fidelity Bayesian Optimization using historical high-fidelity data and task descriptors to improve optimization when highest-fidelity queries are too costly [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Out-Of-The-Loop Multi-Fidelity Bayesian Optimization
items.summary:
Multi-fidelity Bayesian optimization (MF-BO) typically leverages correlations across different fidelity levels to optimize expensive black-box functions. However, in many real-world scenarios, querying the highest-fidelity function is prohibitively expensive, though practitioners often have access to historical high-fidelity data from previous experiments. This work identifies the suboptimality of standard MF-BO algorithms under these conditions and introduces a method that incorporates historical high-fidelity observations along with task descriptors, which can be explicit or extracted from metadata, to enhance optimization performance.

The proposed approach is validated on synthetic benchmarks and real-world applications including molecular optimization and hyperparameter tuning. By integrating prior high-fidelity data outside the optimization loop, the method addresses practical challenges where the true objective function cannot be frequently evaluated, demonstrating improved effectiveness over traditional MF-BO techniques.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.04113v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Black-box optimization is a ubiquitous problem in science and engineering, often dealing with expensive objective functions with cheaper lower-fidelity proxies available. Multi-fidelity Bayesian optimization (MF-BO) is a principled approach to this problem, leveraging correlations across different fidelities when querying the objective. However, for many important MF-BO tasks, the true highest-fidelity function is prohibitively expensive to be part of the optimization loop. Nevertheless, practitioners often have gold standard data (observations of the highest-fidelity function) obtained from previous experiments that might provide information for the current task. For instance, in molecular optimization, chemists often pick the top-$k$ candidate molecules using various computer simulations, and later reveal their true objective function values. In this work, we demonstrate the suboptimality of standard MF-BO algorithms in the real-world scenarios above, even under ideal assumptions. Next, we mitigate this problem by incorporating historical high-fidelity data accompanied by task descriptors---which can be explicitly given or extracted from unstructured metadata. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our methods on synthetic functions, as well as real-world problems in chemistry and hyperparameter optimization.

items.summary: Researchers propose InvFlowFD, a novel music perceptual quality metric that eliminates the need for paired noisy-clean data and background sets by leveraging a pre-trained Flow Matching backbone. items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.04142v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Existing reference-free methods for evaluating music perceptual quality alleviate the need for paired noisy-clean data, but they still rely on a background set, which is used to compute aggregated statistics of clean audio samples. In this work, we propose a novel approach that eliminates this requirement, achieving background-set-free and reference-free quality estimation using only a pre-trained Flow Matching backbone. We demonstrate that unconditional Flow Matching inversion via simple Euler integration is sufficient to detect various artificial distortions and accurately rank music generation models against human perceptual judgments. We introduce InvFlowFD, which performs flow inversion and compares a group of inverted samples to the prior distribution. We evaluate our method against prior work, quantitatively and with a thorough human study. Results suggest that InvFlowFD is highly correlated with human perception of sound distortions, as well as generative models' quality, while being more flexible and less restrictive than existing metrics.

items.title: Researchers introduce LiNC, a lightweight noise correction method using per-sample trust parameters and Gaussian Mixture Modeling to improve label noise handling in medical imaging datasets [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: LiNC: Lightweight Noise Correction via Per-Sample Trust and Gaussian Mixture Modeling
items.summary:
Label noise in medical imaging datasets, caused by factors like inter-rater variability and annotation errors, can reduce the reliability of machine learning models. To address this, researchers developed Lightweight Noise Correction (LiNC), which assigns a trainable trust parameter to each training sample to balance reliance on observed labels versus model predictions during training. LiNC uses a Gaussian Mixture Model to classify samples as clean, ambiguous, or noisy and applies correction phases accordingly, improving accuracy and mislabel detection on ten 2D MedMNISTv2 datasets with up to 50% label noise.

LiNC maintains training efficiency with negligible overhead, as its complexity remains dominated by the base network and memory usage grows linearly with the training set size. This approach offers a practical solution for enhancing model robustness against label noise in clinical imaging applications.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.04147v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Label noise is common in medical imaging datasets due to factors such as inter-rater variability, annotation errors, and ambiguous cases. This can severely undermine the reliability and clinical effectiveness of machine learning models trained using those datasets. To address this challenge, we introduce Lightweight Noise Correction (LiNC), which adds a single trainable trust parameter per training sample and learns when to use the observed label and when to defer to the model during a standard training loop. The key idea is to train using a convex combination of the observed label and the model's own predictive distribution, controlled by a per-sample trust parameter. We show that the gradient of this objective drives trust values in opposite directions for clean versus noisy samples in the early training phase, yielding separable trust distributions. We use a 3-component Gaussian Mixture Model over the trust values to separate them into clean, ambiguous, and noisy cases and then execute a short soft-correction phase on the noisy cases and a final hard correction phase. Experiments on ten 2D datasets from MedMNISTv2 under label noise of up to 50% show consistent gains in accuracy and strong mislabel detection. LiNC adds negligible asymptotic overhead: the training-time complexity remains dominated by the base network, with additional memory growing linearly with the size of the training set.

items.title: Researchers introduce Trident, an agentic LLM framework that breaks deep reinforcement learning cyber defenses by reducing blue agent performance by 522% using adaptive attack strategies [ * ] [ ⬢ ]
items.originalTitle: Trident : How to Break Deep Reinforcement Learning Cyber Defenses (Agentic)
items.summary:
Researchers present Trident, a new agentic large language model (LLM) red teaming framework designed to evaluate and challenge autonomous cyber defense systems based on deep reinforcement learning (DRL). Trident includes a dynamic benchmark environment, a dataset of over 13,000 red-blue interaction trajectories, and a novel "Code-as-Policy" architecture that trains adaptive red agents to generate and execute attack strategies against DRL defenders.

The framework's trainable planner autonomously discovers sophisticated attack behaviors such as decoy avoidance and adaptive state prioritization, which static heuristic red agents fail to uncover. Empirical tests show that Trident significantly degrades the defensive performance of existing DRL-based cyber defense agents, revealing fundamental vulnerabilities in current autonomous defense approaches.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.04317v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Autonomous cyber defense systems based on Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) have attracted significant research attention, yet remain evaluated almost exclusively against static, heuristic red agents, leaving their robustness against adaptive threats critically understudied. Meanwhile, recent advances in Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) have improved LLM reasoning, but their integration into cybersecurity remains elusive due to the absence of suitable benchmark environments and interaction datasets. To bridge this gap, we introduce Trident, an agentic LLM red teaming framework comprising three components: a dynamic benchmark with isolated sandbox servers spanning CybORG CAGE 4 and CyberWheel, a dataset comprises over 13,000 high-fidelity red-blue interaction trajectories for RLVR, and a ``Code-as-Policy'' RLVR agentic architecture Trident Agentic). The latter reformulates red agent training as a contextual bandit via a tripartite Log Summarizer--Planner--Coder design, where a trainable Planner generates complete attack strategies from compressed execution logs, which a frozen Coder translates into executable Python policies deployed against live DRL defenders. Empirical evaluations reveal a fundamental brittleness in existing defenses: with a single trainable 7B planner, Trident reduces blue agent defensive performance by an average of 522% compared to static red agent baselines while autonomously discovering emergent behaviors such as decoy avoidance and adaptive state prioritization that static heuristics entirely fail to uncover.

items.title: Researchers propose Lexi-LowGLM, an efficient online algorithm for generalized low-rank matrix bandits with multiple prioritized objectives using lexicographic preference order [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Efficient Online Lexicographic Generalized Low-Rank Matrix Bandits
items.summary: This paper introduces Lexi-LowGLM, an online algorithm designed for generalized low-rank matrix bandits where multiple objectives have different priority levels evaluated lexicographically. The method estimates objective-specific low-rank subspaces and updates estimators via an online Newton step, reducing update complexity from quadratic to linear over time. The authors establish a regret bound dependent on the effective low-rank dimension rather than the ambient dimension, and numerical experiments demonstrate the algorithm's effectiveness and computational efficiency.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.04324v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper studies generalized low-rank matrix bandits with multiple prioritized objectives. At each round, the learner selects a matrix-valued arm and observes a vector-valued reward, whose components correspond to multiple objectives with different priority levels. Each objective is governed by an objective-specific generalized low-rank matrix model, and the learner evaluates arms according to a lexicographic preference order, prioritizing higher-level objectives before lower-level ones. We propose \textsc{Lexi-LowGLM}, an efficient online algorithm that first estimates objective-specific low-rank subspaces and then performs lexicographic learning in the reduced feature spaces. Unlike existing single-objective algorithms that repeatedly solve a batch generalized linear estimator using all historical observations, \textsc{Lexi-LowGLM} updates each objective-specific estimator via an online Newton step, reducing the estimator-update complexity over $T$ rounds from $O(T^2)$ to $O(T)$. We establish a regret bound of $\widetilde O\left(W_i^{\rm lex}\sqrt{m}\,(d_1+d_2)r\sqrt{T}\right)$ for each objective $i\in[m]$, where $r$ is an upper bound on the ranks of the objective-specific parameter matrices and $W_i^{\rm lex}$ characterizes the lexicographic trade-off effect. This bound depends on the effective low-rank dimension $(d_1+d_2)r$ rather than the ambient dimension $d_1d_2$. Numerical experiments further validate the effectiveness and computational efficiency of the proposed method.

Evaluated on spatial navigation tasks, it structurally decouples transition dynamics from reward signals, enabling near-instantaneous adaptation to new goals and positive backward transfer. items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.04334v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Contemporary model-free reinforcement learning algorithms can achieve very high performance, but have low sample efficiency and are not robust to changes in the environment. Model-based algorithms have much higher sample efficiency, but still fail when the environment shifts. This paper introduces Adaptive Topological Learning with Abstract Successors (ATLAS) to combat these challenges. ATLAS uses a Grow When Required network with Successor Features in order to achieve high sample efficiency while also robustly tackling catastrophic forgetting. We evaluate ATLAS in spatial navigation tasks, benchmarking its performance against common on-policy and off-policy algorithms. Our empirical results demonstrate that by structurally decoupling transition dynamics from the reward signal, ATLAS achieves near-instantaneous adaptation to new goals and can exhibit positive backward transfer, significantly outperforming baseline methods in non-stationary environments.

items.title: Researchers propose HyperTrust framework to improve hypergraph neural network robustness against label noise with trustworthiness estimation and structure adjustment [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Towards Trustworthy Hypergraph Neural Networks under Label Noise
items.summary:
Researchers present a systematic study on hypergraph node classification under label noise, adapting existing learning methods and revealing their limitations. They propose HyperTrust, a framework that estimates hyperedge trustworthiness and uses modules to enhance reliable supervision and suppress noise, improving prediction accuracy.

HyperTrust combines a pretraining-based, entropy-aware strategy with HyperedgeBoost and HyperedgePrune modules to connect unlabeled nodes to trustworthy hyperedges and remove noisy connections. Experiments and theoretical analysis demonstrate its effectiveness across multiple hypergraph datasets and noisy conditions, providing a unified benchmark and foundation for future research in hypergraph learning with label noise.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.04377v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Hypergraph neural networks (HGNNs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in processing complex higher-order relationships. However, their performance is highly dependent on labeled data, making them vulnerable to label noise. Despite advances in learning with label noise (LLN) and graph learning with label noise (GLN), noisy-label learning on hypergraphs remains underexplored. In this paper, we present a systematic study of hypergraph node classification under label noise. First, we adapt representative LLN and GLN methods to hypergraphs and evaluate them under a unified benchmark, revealing the limitations of existing robust learning strategies for hypergraphs. Building on this, we propose a new hypergraph robust framework, HyperTrust, which first estimates hyperedge trustworthiness through a pretraining-based, entropy-aware strategy, and then incorporates the HyperedgeBoost module to enhance reliable supervision by connecting unlabeled nodes to trustworthy hyperedges, as well as the HyperedgePrune module to suppress noisy propagation by removing untrustworthy node-hyperedge incidences. Finally, two modules work collaboratively to adjust the hypergraph structure and generate final predictions. Extensive experiments and theoretical analysis demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of HyperTrust on multiple hypergraph datasets under various noisy settings. Our work provides a unified benchmark and an effective solution for hypergraph learning with label noise and lays a foundation for future research in this direction.

items.title: NodeJEPA introduces structure-conditioned latent prediction for node-level graph self-supervised learning without input reconstruction or handcrafted augmentations [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: NodeJEPA: Structure-Conditioned Latent Prediction for Node-Level Graph Self-Supervised Learning
items.summary: NodeJEPA is a joint-embedding predictive architecture designed for node-level graph self-supervised learning that predicts latent representations of masked k-hop ego-subgraphs using a context encoder and a target encoder updated via exponential moving average. The model incorporates a structure-conditioned predictor that uses spectral and centrality descriptors through cross-attention, along with variance, covariance, and Laplacian spectral regularizers to stabilize embedding geometry, and optionally employs a curriculum to increase masking difficulty during training. Evaluated on standard node classification benchmarks with linear probing and fine-tuning, NodeJEPA offers a practical approach to node-level JEPA-style latent prediction and clarifies the benefits of structural conditioning in representation learning; its code and evaluation scripts are publicly available.
